title: Nondegenerate simplex subcategory is a poset with unique factorization
statement: Use simplicial sets, standard simplices and ordinary nerves of [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones]. Let $X$ be a small simplicial set. A simplex is nondegenerate if it is not obtained from a lower-dimensional simplex by a nonidentity surjective simplex operator. Suppose every nondegenerate simplex $\Delta^n\to X$ is a monomorphism, meaning injective in every degree. Let $\mathsf S(X)$ be the ordinary category whose objects are all simplices $\sigma:\Delta^n\to X$ and whose morphisms $\sigma\to\tau$ are monotone maps $\alpha:[n]\to[m]$ satisfying $\tau\Delta(\alpha)=\sigma$, with composition of monotone maps. Let $B_X$ be the full subcategory on the nondegenerate simplices. Then there is at most one morphism between any two objects of $B_X$, every such morphism is represented by an injective monotone map, and existence of a morphism defines a partial order on its objects. For any simplex $\sigma$, write $\sigma=\bar\sigma\Delta(s_\sigma)$ for its unique nondegenerate decomposition of [lem-weil-pbc-simplicial-set-nondegenerate-decomposition], with $s_\sigma$ surjective. Every morphism $\alpha:\sigma\to\tau$ with $\tau$ nondegenerate factors uniquely as $\sigma\xrightarrow{s_\sigma}\bar\sigma\xrightarrow{t}\tau$; that is, $\alpha=t\circ s_\sigma$ with $\tau\Delta(t)=\bar\sigma$.

source.place: HTT Variant 4.2.3.15, step (5), printed p. 256; the nondegenerate-simplex and dimension argument is expanded here. Online source read 2026-10-17; archival copy WANTED.

proof.text: Let $\sigma:\Delta^n\to X$ and $\tau:\Delta^m\to X$ be nondegenerate, and suppose $\alpha,\beta:[n]\to[m]$ represent arrows $\sigma\to\tau$. By [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones], the vertices of $\Delta^n$ are the maps $[0]\to[n]$, and $\Delta(\alpha)$ acts on them by $i\mapsto\alpha(i)$. For each $i$, the arrow equations give $\tau_0(\alpha(i))=\sigma_0(i)=\tau_0(\beta(i))$. The hypothesis that $\tau$ is injective in every degree gives injectivity of $\tau_0$, hence $\alpha(i)=\beta(i)$ for every $i$. Thus $\alpha=\beta$, proving that every hom-set of $B_X$ has at most one element.

source.place: Variant 4.2.3.15 (5), uniqueness of faces; Variant 4.2.3.16 (*); explicit agent expansion, online PDF read 2026-10-17; local archival copy WANTED.

proof.text: For an arrow $\alpha:\sigma\to\tau$ with $\sigma$ nondegenerate, suppose $\alpha:[n]\to[m]$ is not injective. There are $i<j$ with $\alpha(i)=\alpha(j)$; monotonicity gives $\alpha(i)=\alpha(i+1)$, and $n\geq1$. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-simplex-degeneracy-factorization] with $k=n$, target ordinal $[m]$ and this index $i$. It gives $\alpha=\psi\circ q_i$, where $q_i:[n]\to[n-1]$ collapses $i,i+1$. Consequently $\sigma=\tau\Delta(\psi)\Delta(q_i)$ is the degeneracy of the lower-dimensional simplex $\tau\Delta(\psi)$ by a nonidentity surjection. This contradicts the definition of nondegenerate. Hence every arrow of $B_X$ is injective; if $n=0$, injectivity already holds because the domain has one element.

source.place: Variant 4.2.3.15 (5), face operators on nondegenerate simplices; explicit agent expansion, online PDF read 2026-10-17; local archival copy WANTED.

proof.text: Define $\sigma\leq\tau$ when an arrow $\sigma\to\tau$ exists. Identity and composition of the monotone maps defining $\mathsf S(X)$ give reflexivity and transitivity. If arrows exist both ways, step 2 gives injections $[n]\to[m]$ and $[m]\to[n]$, hence $n=m$. A monotone injection $[n]\to[n]$ lists $n+1$ distinct elements of that same ordered set in increasing order, so its list is $0,1,\ldots,n$ and it is the identity. The arrow equation then gives $\sigma=\tau$ as maps from the same standard simplex. This proves antisymmetry on the actual objects, not merely on isomorphism classes. Together with step 1, $B_X$ is the category associated with this partial order.

source.place: Variant 4.2.3.15 (5), conclusion that the nondegenerate-simplex category is a poset; explicit agent expansion, online PDF read 2026-10-17; local archival copy WANTED.

proof.text: Now let $\sigma:\Delta^n\to X$ be any simplex. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-simplicial-set-nondegenerate-decomposition] to its top simplex $z=\sigma_n(\mathrm{id}_{[n]})$. It supplies a unique $r$, a nondegenerate $y\in X_r$ and a surjective monotone $s:[n]\to[r]$ with $z=X(s)(y)$. To translate this into maps, define $\bar\sigma_d(u)=X(u)(y)$ for $u:[d]\to[r]$. Functoriality gives a simplicial map. Naturality of $\sigma$ gives $\sigma_d(v)=X(v)(z)$ for every $v:[d]\to[n]$, so $\sigma=\bar\sigma\Delta(s)$. Evaluation at the identity also translates uniqueness back to uniqueness of $\bar\sigma$ and $s$. These are precisely the $\bar\sigma$ and $s_\sigma$ of the statement; write $s=s_\sigma$. The standard-simplex formulas here are those of [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones].

source.place: Variant 4.2.3.16, left-adjoint assertion after condition (*): choose the nondegenerate core; explicit agent expansion, online PDF read 2026-10-17; local archival copy WANTED.

proof.text: Let $\alpha:[n]\to[m]$ represent an arrow $\sigma\to\tau$ with $\tau$ nondegenerate. For each $j\in[r]$, put $a(j)=\min s^{-1}(j)$. These minima exist because $s$ is surjective. If $j<j\prime$, every element of $s^{-1}(j)$ precedes every element of $s^{-1}(j\prime)$ by monotonicity, so $a$ is monotone and $sa=\mathrm{id}_{[r]}$. Define $t=\alpha a$. If $s(i)=s(i\prime)$, the two equations for $\sigma$ imply $\tau_0(\alpha(i))=\bar\sigma_0(s(i))=\bar\sigma_0(s(i\prime))=\tau_0(\alpha(i\prime))$. Since $\tau_0$ is injective, $\alpha(i)=\alpha(i\prime)$. Taking $i\prime=a(s(i))$ gives $\alpha=t s$. Finally, using composition of standard-simplex operators [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones], $\tau\Delta(t)=\tau\Delta(\alpha)\Delta(a)=\sigma\Delta(a)=\bar\sigma\Delta(sa)=\bar\sigma$. Thus $t$ is an arrow $\bar\sigma\to\tau$ in $B_X$, and gives the required factorization.

source.place: Variant 4.2.3.16, left-adjoint assertion: explicit section and factorization; explicit agent expansion, online PDF read 2026-10-17; local archival copy WANTED.

proof.text: If $t\prime:[r]\to[m]$ is another monotone map satisfying $\alpha=t\prime s$, then for each $j\in[r]$ the section from step 5 gives $t\prime(j)=t\prime(s(a(j)))=\alpha(a(j))=t(j)$. Therefore $t\prime=t$. Both $\bar\sigma$ and $\tau$ are nondegenerate, so step 2 also shows that this unique arrow is injective. The factorization is through the fixed unique decomposition of step 4, hence establishes exactly the final clause of the statement.
